title: Credentialing and Re-Credentialing Management Playbook
audience: Practice administrators and revenue cycle managers at independent practices who own the credentialing function (stated on the cover and in the introduction); the closing note addresses 'independent practice teams'. Not written for physician-owners, credentialing specialists or facility-based practices.
summary: An operational guide to running provider credentialing and payer enrollment as a calendar-driven system rather than from memory. It covers credentialing basics, the CAQH profile and its 120-day attestation cycle, Medicare enrollment and five-year revalidation, and the 36-month commercial re-credentialing cycle. The central method is one named owner running two linked tools: a provider-by-payer calendar with internal triggers set ahead of each deadline (day 90 for CAQH, six months for re-credentialing) and a live status tracker refreshed through follow-up with each payer every two weeks. Around that core sit a nine-step initial enrollment sequence, a backward-planned onboarding timeline for new hires, a payer timeline table, a 72-hour protocol for enrollment gaps, a six-domain annual audit that includes exclusion screening, five KPIs, a 90-day rollout plan and two checklists. No sources are cited, and Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, facility privileging and non-physician practitioners are absent.

outline.gist: Cover, contents with page numbers off by one, and a disclaimer saying figures are public ranges or vendor-observed patterns; no sources.
Lapses go unnoticed until denials arrive 30 to 60 days later; argues for a documented calendar instead of memory; explains reading order.
Defines credentialing, primary source verification, the 36-month standard, CAQH's 120-day attestation, consequences of three lapse types, and core vocabulary.

outline.section: Section 2: CAQH ProView - The Universal Profile
outline.gist: Profile contents, supporting documents, 120-day attestation with a 90-day internal reminder, practice-manager access; ends with PECOS 2.0 and Medicare revalidation.
Lead times by payer, Medicare effective-date rule, document package, CAQH payer authorization, and nine steps ending with group NPI linkage.
Separate 36-month clocks per payer, unreliable payer notices, seven calendar fields, six-month internal trigger, and how CAQH currency protects re-credentialing.
Ten tracker fields, follow-up every two weeks with a logged trail, one named owner, and a practice-side credentialing file per provider.
Backward timeline from 120 to 30 days before start, claim holds for pending payers, the CAQH authorization trap, and a locum billing caution.

outline.section: Section 7: Payer-Specific Credentialing Requirements and Timelines
outline.gist: Short entries for Medicare, UnitedHealthcare, Aetna, Cigna, Blue Cross Blue Shield and Medicaid, expedited credentialing, and a one-page comparison table.
Establish the gap date, six actions in 72 hours, written retroactive-coverage requests, patient communication, and an audit after resolution.
Twenty-eight checkbox items in six domains: CAQH, PECOS, commercial calendar, recent hires, exclusion monitoring, file currency; annual and event-triggered.
Five KPIs with targets and warning signals, to be reported in the monthly revenue cycle report seen by the owner.
Month 1 baseline audit and owner assignment; Month 2 build tracker, reminders, files and screening; Month 3 operate, review with owner, add KPIs.
A 21-item new-provider checklist by phase and a 14-item monthly, quarterly and annual calendar maintenance checklist.

outline.section: Closing: The Calendar Is the System
outline.gist: Restates the thesis in slogans, repeats the four-month gap illustration, and points to other CleanClaimRx products.
Repeats the disclaimer: educational only, figures unsourced, confirm with payers and advisers.

processes.name: Initial payer enrollment sequence
steps: Confirm an active individual NPI in NPPES
Complete and attest the CAQH profile with current documents
Authorize each target payer to view the CAQH profile
File Medicare enrollment and record the filing date
File Medicaid enrollment for each state served
Submit commercial applications in order of patient volume
Log submission dates, payer contacts and expected completion
Confirm receipt at 15 days, then follow up every two weeks
Confirm individual-to-group linkage at every payer before the first visit
processes.owner_role: Credentialing owner (office or billing manager in a small practice; dedicated coordinator in a larger one)
processes.cadence: Per new provider; begin at least 120 days before the start date (see accuracy concern on Medicare timing)

processes.name: CAQH profile maintenance
steps: Keep every profile section complete
Upload renewed licence, DEA, malpractice and board documents when they renew
Re-attest on a 90-day internal reminder, ahead of the 120-day deadline
Confirm payer access authorizations for every active payer
Keep practice-manager access to each provider's profile
processes.owner_role: Credentialing owner, with the provider attesting
processes.cadence: Every 90 days, plus whenever a document renews

processes.name: Re-credentialing calendar management
steps: List every provider-payer pair with effective date and due date
Set an internal trigger six months before each due date
Track CAQH attestation and Medicare revalidation dates as separate lines
Review monthly for deadlines inside the next 12 months
Check Medicare revalidation dates on the CMS list quarterly
Start packet assembly at the trigger without waiting for a payer notice
processes.cadence: Monthly review; quarterly Medicare check; annual completeness check

processes.name: Application status tracking and payer follow-up
steps: Record each application with type, submission date and payer contact
Contact the payer every two weeks until approval
Ask whether the file is complete and whether any document request is open
Escalate any application idle in queue for 30 days
Log date, person reached, status reported and next follow-up date
Record the effective date on approval
processes.cadence: Every two weeks per open application

processes.name: New-provider onboarding (backward timeline)
steps: At 120 days: NPI, CAQH, payer authorizations, Medicare, Medicaid and commercial submissions, group linkage
At 90 days: start two-week follow-up cycle, recheck CAQH status, plan for payers that will be late
At 60 days: reconfirm every application, request expedited review, confirm Medicare filing date
At 30 days: list pending payers, brief staff, set claim holds for pending payers
At start: confirm active versus pending, add provider to calendar and exclusion screening

processes.name: Credentialing gap response (first 72 hours)
steps: Get the exact lapse date from the payer
Pull all claims with service dates on or after that date, by payer
Check CAQH status and re-attest if expired
File re-enrollment and request expedited review in writing
File Medicare reactivation the same day
Hold new claims to the affected payer and notify staff
Request retroactive coverage in writing with a documented timeline
Tell affected patients what happened and do not bill them for gap-caused amounts
Run the full audit once the gap is closed
processes.owner_role: Credentialing owner or revenue cycle manager

processes.name: Credentialing compliance audit (six domains)
steps: Verify CAQH status, documents, authorizations and manager access
Verify Medicare enrollment, revalidation dates and reassignments
Verify commercial effective dates, due dates, triggers and group linkage
Recheck providers hired in the last 24 months at every payer
Run and log exclusion checks and confirm a monthly policy exists
Verify file documents against the underlying policies and licences
processes.owner_role: Credentialing owner, reporting to the administrator or physician-owner
processes.cadence: At least annually; immediately after a gap, provider departure, payer contract change or ownership change

processes.name: Monthly monitoring and reporting routine
steps: Screen every provider against the OIG exclusion list and SAM.gov and log date and result
Review CAQH attestation status for every provider
Pull enrollment-related denial codes from the billing system
Update the tracker for all open applications
Report the five credentialing KPIs in the monthly revenue cycle report
processes.cadence: Monthly (the checklist puts the denial-code review quarterly)

metrics.name: Days to Complete New Provider Credentialing
metrics.definition: Calendar days from first CAQH profile submission until every target payer is confirmed active.
metrics.formula: date last target payer confirmed active minus date of initial CAQH profile submission (implied; not written as a formula)
metrics.target: All priority payers credentialed within 120 days of application submission; no provider sees patients until Medicare and the top three commercial payers are confirmed active.
metrics.red_flag: Any new-provider application past 90 days without payer approval; escalation should start at 90 days.

metrics.name: CAQH Attestation Compliance Rate
metrics.definition: Share of provider CAQH profiles attested within the practice's 90-day internal standard rather than the 120-day CAQH deadline.
metrics.formula: profiles attested by day 90 / all provider profiles (implied; not written as a formula)
metrics.red_flag: Any profile reaching day 100 without attestation, leaving 20 days before the CAQH deadline.

metrics.name: Re-Credentialing Applications Submitted Within Six-Month Window
metrics.definition: Share of re-credentialing applications submitted to the payer at least six months before the re-credentialing deadline.
metrics.formula: applications submitted six or more months early / all re-credentialing applications due (implied; not written as a formula)
metrics.red_flag: Any re-credentialing deadline inside six months with no application already in progress.

metrics.name: Credentialing Denial Rate
metrics.definition: Share of total denials carrying a provider-not-enrolled or equivalent credentialing-gap denial code, pulled monthly. No specific codes are named.
metrics.formula: credentialing-coded denials / total denials (implied; not written as a formula)
metrics.red_flag: Any credentialing denial; a sudden rise signals that a gap has opened.

metrics.name: Time in Credentialing Gap (Annual)
metrics.definition: Total provider-days in the calendar year during which any provider was in a documented credentialing gap with any payer.
metrics.formula: sum of (gap resolution date minus gap start date) across every provider and payer affected (implied; not written as a formula)
metrics.red_flag: Any non-zero value triggers an immediate review of the credentialing system.

numeric_claims.claim: Enrollment-lapse denials begin arriving 30 to 60 days after the lapse.
Most commercial payers require re-credentialing every two to three years.
CAQH ProView requires re-attestation every 120 days.
A provider unable to bill for four months of a year generates roughly 33 percent of expected revenue for that period (illustration).
Primary source verification typically takes 60 to 120 days for commercial payers and 30 to 45 days for Medicare.
NCQA standards require re-credentialing at least every 36 months.

numeric_claims.claim: Illinois uses a 180-day CAQH re-attestation window and is the only state that differs from 120 days.
Some payers send re-credentialing notices 90 to 120 days ahead; others 30 days out or not at all.
Medicare revalidation is required every 5 years, and every 3 years for DMEPOS suppliers.
More than 900 health plans access CAQH data.
The CAQH ProView profile has 18 data sections.
Work history must show no unexplained employment gaps exceeding three months.
CMS launched PECOS 2.0 in late 2025, replacing the legacy portal.
Revalidation due dates are posted on the Medicare Revalidation List at data.cms.gov seven months before the deadline.
Aetna averages 60 to 90 days for initial credentialing.
Cigna averages 45 to 90 days for initial credentialing.
UnitedHealthcare averages 60 to 90 days (Section 3) but typically 45 to 90 days (Section 7 and table).
Blue Cross Blue Shield plans currently range from 60 to 120 days by state.
Medicare PECOS enrollment typically runs 30 to 45 days from a complete application.
Medicare permits retroactive billing for up to 30 days before the enrollment effective date.
Start commercial credentialing at least 120 days before a provider's start date and Medicare enrollment 90 days out.
A complete, attested CAQH profile shortens credentialing timelines by 30 to 45 days.
Skipping the CAQH payer authorization step costs two to four weeks.
NPI registration typically takes 2 to 3 weeks.
The UnitedHealthcare Credentialing Plan 2025-2027 sets 36-month re-credentialing cycles for Licensed Independent Practitioners.
numeric_claims.source_cited: UnitedHealthcare Credentialing Plan 2025-2027 named; no link or page

numeric_claims.claim: Six providers credentialed with eight payers each produce 48 re-credentialing events across a three-year window.
CAQH attestation must be completed within 14 days of submitting the UnitedHealthcare enrollment application.
Most state Medicaid programs take 45 to 90 days for initial enrollment.
The OIG exclusion list updates monthly.
Credentialing platforms suit practices with four or more providers; the CAQH practice-manager module suits more than two.

checkable_claims.claim: Claims submitted during a Medicare deactivation period are not retroactively compensable after billing privileges are reactivated; the gap is a permanent revenue loss, not a delay.
checkable_claims.why: Medicare fee-for-service is about 55% of charges. If true, one missed revalidation creates an unrecoverable loss, which sets how much control the revalidation date deserves. Check 42 CFR 424.540 and 424.555, plus the rebuttal right and the 2024 stay-of-enrollment step the document omits.

checkable_claims.claim: Medicare sets the effective date as the later of the application filing date or the date services first began at the enrolled location; retroactive billing is permitted up to 30 days prior when circumstances precluded advance enrollment.
checkable_claims.why: Fixes the first billable date for any new physician or nurse practitioner and how long claims can safely be held. A wrong date means unpaid visits or a needlessly delayed start. Check 42 CFR 424.520(d) and 424.521(a), including the 90-day disaster exception the document omits.

checkable_claims.claim: Start commercial payer credentialing a minimum of 120 days before a new provider is scheduled to see patients. Start Medicare enrollment 90 days out. [Onboarding table: submit Medicare PECOS enrollment 120 days before start.]
checkable_claims.why: As I understand 42 CFR 424.526(a) and Program Integrity Manual chapter 10, a contractor may return a practitioner application received more than 60 days before the effective date listed. Filing at 90 to 120 days could cost the very filing date the playbook says to protect.

checkable_claims.claim: Most providers revalidate Medicare enrollment every five years (DMEPOS suppliers every three); due dates are published on the Medicare Revalidation List at data.cms.gov and are updated seven months before the deadline.
checkable_claims.why: The look-ahead window sets how often the practice must check the list and how early it may file. If dates post later than stated a quarterly check could miss them; if a revalidation is filed too early it may be returned as unsolicited.

checkable_claims.claim: CMS launched PECOS 2.0 in late 2025, replacing the legacy enrollment portal; legacy PECOS credentials and workflows do not transfer automatically and the transition requires account re-configuration.
checkable_claims.why: The audit and 90-day plan send the practice to reconfigure access on this premise. If the launch date is wrong or existing Identity & Access logins carry over, those steps are wasted and the document's claim to be current fails; if right, access must be tested before any revalidation.

checkable_claims.claim: CAQH ProView requires re-attestation every 120 days; a profile not attested within 120 days moves to Expired status. Illinois operates on a 180-day window, the only state with a different standard.
checkable_claims.why: The whole CAQH calendar rests on this interval, and UnitedHealthcare, Humana and Florida Blue draw on CAQH. Also confirm the product name: CAQH renamed ProView the Provider Data Portal in 2023, so the login address and terms in the playbook may be stale.

checkable_claims.claim: Medicare allows billing under the supervising physician's NPI for locum arrangements that meet the Q6 modifier requirements.
checkable_claims.why: Q6 is, as I understand it, the fee-for-time rule for a substitute physician covering an absent regular physician for no more than 60 continuous days, and it does not extend to nurse practitioners. Applying it as described in a physician-plus-NP practice risks false claims.

checkable_claims.claim: Medicaid does not grant retroactive effective dates in most circumstances; unlike Medicare, there is generally no retroactive billing right for services before the enrollment effective date.
checkable_claims.why: Florida Medicaid managed care and dual-eligible patients are in the payer mix. Retroactivity is state law; Florida's statute (s. 409.907), as I recall it, ties the effective date to receipt of the application. If the blanket statement is wrong, recoverable claims would be written off.

adopt.idea: One provider-by-payer calendar holding every expiring item: plan re-credentialing dates, CAQH attestation, Medicare revalidation, licence, DEA, malpractice and board certification.
adopt.why: The deadlines live in different systems on different cycles; a single register is the only way an owner, an agent or a successor can see them all.
adopt.note: Add what the playbook leaves out: Medicare Advantage plans, Florida Medicaid and its managed-care plans, VA and Tricare networks, hospital and facility privileges, and the nurse practitioner's protocol documents.

adopt.idea: Internal triggers set well ahead of external deadlines: day 90 for the 120-day CAQH attestation, six months for plan re-credentialing, a 12-month look-ahead flag.
adopt.why: Buffers absorb absence, lost notices and payer delay, and cost almost nothing to automate.
adopt.note: Read the six-month trigger as 'make the file ready and watch for the plan's request'; most plans start re-credentialing themselves and will not take a packet that early.

adopt.idea: Update CAQH documents the day a licence, DEA registration or malpractice policy renews instead of waiting for the next attestation.
adopt.why: Stale documents are the usual cause of mid-cycle document requests and stalled files.
adopt.note: Suits an AI agent: watch renewal dates, fetch the new certificate, stage the upload, then have the provider attest.

adopt.idea: One named owner for credentialing, plus a practice-side file per provider holding current documents and the enrollment history with every payer.
adopt.why: Removes dependence on one person's memory, makes the function auditable, and is something a buyer will ask to see.
adopt.note: Where agents do the work, still name an accountable human; attestations are the provider's own legal statements and should not be made without the provider's review.

adopt.idea: Live application tracker with payer contact every two weeks and a logged trail of date, person, status and next action.
adopt.why: Applications stall silently; the log is the evidence when a payer says a request was sent.
adopt.note: Needed whenever a provider, location, tax ID or plan is added.

adopt.idea: Verify individual-to-group linkage (Medicare reassignment, plan group affiliation) explicitly before the first claim.
adopt.why: An approved individual enrollment without group linkage pays out of network or denies.
adopt.note: Worth checking for both clinicians across all plans now; the playbook's CMS-855R reference looks dated, so use the current PECOS reassignment workflow.

adopt.idea: Pull Medicare revalidation due dates from the CMS list on a fixed schedule instead of waiting for the contractor's letter.
adopt.why: A missed revalidation leads to deactivation and unpaid services for the gap period.
adopt.note: The highest-value control here given the Medicare share. Check individual and group records, and add the duty to report enrollment changes to Medicare on time, which the playbook omits.

adopt.idea: Backward-planned onboarding timeline for a new clinician, with a plan for payers that will not be ready and claim holds for them.
adopt.why: Start-date revenue depends on enrollment lead time; planning backward makes the ramp forecast honest.
adopt.note: Relevant when recruiting. Correct the Medicare timing to the window CMS accepts, add facility privileging lead times, and cap claim holds by each plan's timely filing limit.

adopt.idea: Monthly exclusion screening against the OIG list and SAM.gov with a dated log of each check.
adopt.why: Low cost, and the log is what an auditor or plan asks for.
adopt.note: Widen it beyond clinicians to every employee, contractor and vendor, including technology and billing vendors, and add any state Medicaid exclusion list.

adopt.idea: Treat enrollment-related denials as an alarm, report gap days and attestation compliance to the owner monthly, and audit yearly and after any provider departure, contract change or ownership change.
adopt.why: Turns a back-office task into a visible risk measure and gives a ready check before a sale or restructuring.
adopt.note: Define the actual denial reason and remark codes to watch for each payer; the playbook names none.

practice_relevance.why: The calendar, tracker and audit method transfers directly to a two-clinician practice whose billing is run by AI agents, and the Medicare enrollment and revalidation material touches the 55% fee-for-service base. But the payer detail covers Aetna, Cigna and generic Blue plans rather than Humana, Capital Health Plan, Florida Blue, Florida Medicaid managed care, VA or Tricare. Medicare Advantage and nurse practitioners are never mentioned (zero occurrences each), and hospital privileges appear only as a line in the document list, with nothing on hospital or nursing-facility privileging and reappointment, the gating credentials for facility-based work. Most useful if a clinician is hired or if credentialing becomes a module of a practice-optimization service.

accuracy_concerns: Medicare filing lead time: Section 3 says start Medicare enrollment 90 days out, and the Section 6 table and Checklist 1 put the PECOS submission 120 or more days before start. As I understand 42 CFR 424.526(a) and the Program Integrity Manual, a contractor may return a physician or practitioner application received more than 60 days before the effective date listed on it. Following the playbook risks a returned application and a lost filing date.

Locum billing: Q6 is the fee-for-time arrangement in which the absent regular physician bills for a substitute physician, limited to 60 continuous days. The playbook calls this billing under a 'supervising physician', gives no time limit, ignores the reciprocal (Q5) arrangement and does not say the rule excludes nurse practitioners and physician assistants.

Medicare deactivation: the non-payment statement matches my understanding of 42 CFR 424.555(b) and 424.540, but 'no appeal pathway' is overstated. A deactivation can be contested by rebuttal within a short window (42 CFR 424.546), and CMS added a stay-of-enrollment step in 2024 that the playbook never mentions.

Medicaid retroactivity is presented as generally unavailable. This is state law and varies widely; Florida's statute, as I recall it, sets the effective date at receipt of the application and allows retroactive enrollment in defined cases. The blanket statement could cause recoverable claims to be written off.

CAQH authorization is described as payer-by-payer only, 'not a one-time global authorization'. The CAQH portal offers a global release to all organizations the provider is affiliated with or applying to, alongside plan-by-plan selection; the usual failure point is the plan not yet having added the provider to its roster.

The 36-month clock is said to run from the provider's original effective date with each payer. Under NCQA it runs from the last credentialing decision date and resets at each re-credentialing, so a calendar keyed to effective date can run weeks late.

Re-credentialing is framed as a packet the practice submits on its own schedule. At most CAQH-using plans the plan starts the cycle, pulls the profile and asks for missing items; a practice usually cannot submit six months early.
Says a biennial licence renewal 'produces a new license number'. Renewal changes the expiration date, not the number.

Introduction arithmetic: a provider unable to bill for four of twelve months is said to generate about 33% of expected revenue. That is the share lost, not the share generated; 'the rest is written off' is also unsupported.

Exclusion screening is limited to 'every provider'. Federal exposure covers any employee, contractor or vendor paid directly or indirectly from federal programs. 'Monthly monitoring is not optional' overstates federal law: OIG recommends monthly checks; state Medicaid rules and plan contracts are what usually make them mandatory.

Says billing during a known gap creates compliance exposure but never names the real false-claims risk: billing an unenrolled clinician's services under another clinician's NPI outside valid incident-to or substitute-physician rules.
Claim-hold advice ignores timely filing. Holding claims for a pending Medicare Advantage or Medicaid plan with a short filing limit can forfeit payment as surely as a denial.

Unsupported specifics that look invented or rounded: 18 CAQH data sections (eight listed), more than 900 health plans, 30 to 45 days saved by a complete profile, two to four weeks lost to a missing authorization, a UnitedHealthcare 14-day attestation rule, Blue plans outsourcing credentialing to 'Optum or Carelon', NPI issuance in two to three weeks (CMS says online NPPES applications can finish within about 10 days, and they often take far less).

Section 1 says primary source verification itself takes 60 to 120 days (commercial) and 30 to 45 days (Medicare), conflating verification with total processing time; Medicare enrollment is not NCQA-style credentialing at all.

PECOS 2.0 claims (late-2025 launch; old logins and workflows do not carry over) could not be confirmed from my own knowledge. CMS's pre-launch guidance, as I recall it, said existing Identity & Access logins would continue to work. Verify before acting.
internal_contradictions: UnitedHealthcare initial credentialing is 60 to 90 days in Section 3 but 45 to 90 days in Section 7 and the comparison table.

Section 4 says the six-month trigger is when work begins, 'not when the application is submitted'; Metric 3 scores the share of applications submitted to the payer at least six months before the deadline.

Metric 1 targets all priority payers within 120 days with escalation at 90 days, while Sections 3 and 7 say Blue plans routinely take 60 to 120 days 'or beyond'. Its definition starts the clock at CAQH profile submission; its target starts at application submission.

Metric 1 says no provider sees patients until Medicare is confirmed active; Sections 3, 6 and 7 plan around the Medicare filing-date effective date and 30-day look-back, which presume starting before approval with claims held.
Re-credentialing is 'every two to three years' in the Introduction and glossary, but 'most' payers follow 36 months in Section 4.
CAQH warning thresholds differ: Section 9 flags profiles within 30 days of the 120-day deadline (day 90), Checklist 2 flags within 30 days of the 90-day trigger (day 60), Metric 2 warns at day 100.
Credentialing denial codes are to be pulled monthly in Section 10 but sit under the quarterly review in Checklist 2.
The 90-day plan refers to a 'Section 5 template' for the tracker; Section 5 contains only a bulleted field list.
The disclaimer says figures are labeled as industry benchmark or CCRx-observed 'throughout'; exactly one statement in the body (Cigna specialty-code mismatches) carries either label.
Table of contents page numbers are one page early for every section after the Introduction (Section 1 is listed on page 6 and printed on page 7, and so on).
time_sensitive_or_outdated: 'CAQH ProView' and proview.caqh.org: CAQH renamed the product CAQH Provider Data Portal in 2023. A document dated September 2026 that uses the old name throughout suggests recycled older content.

CMS-855R (Section 9 and Checklist 1): to my knowledge CMS retired the stand-alone reassignment form and folded reassignment into the CMS-855I during 2023-2024; in PECOS, reassignment is part of the online application.
PECOS 2.0 statements are time-bound and unverified (launch timing, login carry-over, feature list).
UnitedHealthcare Credentialing Plan 2025-2027 is a versioned document; cycle and terms need rechecking when it is replaced.
Payer timeline ranges are called 'current' with no as-of date or source.
NCQA's 2025 credentialing changes (shorter verification time limits and monthly sanction and exclusion monitoring by plans, as I understand them) are not reflected.
CMS's stay-of-enrollment status (in effect since 2024) and the rebuttal process for deactivations are not reflected.
No mention of the No Surprises Act provider-directory verification duty (roughly every 90 days since 2022), which now drives much plan outreach to practices.
The seven-month posting window for revalidation due dates should be confirmed against the current CMS revalidation page.
ai_generation_signals: Slogan-style sentences and contrast formulas repeated throughout ('The calendar is the system', 'A process owned by everyone is owned by no one', 'It is not X. It is Y.').
Heavy restatement: the 120-day CAQH attestation rule is stated about 19 times, deactivation is raised 12 times and PECOS 2.0 nine times; callout boxes repeat the paragraph above them.
Round, unsourced numbers and a vendor-experience label ('CCRx-observed') with no data behind it; no author, credential, client example or screenshot.
Arithmetic slip in the opening illustration (33% generated versus lost) and inconsistent figures between sections.
Garbled real-world details: a renewed licence getting a new number, 'contact the CAQH portal', onboarding starting when the provider accepts 'not the day the offer letter is signed'.
Promised tools that are only bullet lists (tracker 'template', calendar); no downloadable file, script or letter.
Ten mentions of five other CleanClaimRx titles plus five references to a 'Domain 9' assessment framework, written as catalog upsell.
Layout padding: 38 pages for about 10,000 words, several near-empty pages, contents page numbers off by one.
Stale product names (ProView, CMS-855R) mixed with a few 'current' hooks (PECOS 2.0, a 2025-2027 plan title) to signal freshness.
missing_for_real_use: Medicare Advantage: plan credentialing, how it differs from fee-for-service enrollment, and plan-specific timely filing.
Medicaid managed care and dual-eligibles: state enrollment as a precondition for plan participation, crossover claims, state revalidation.

Guidance for any plan beyond four national commercial payers: Humana appears once in a list; Capital Health Plan, Florida Blue, VA Community Care, Tricare and Railroad Medicare not at all; nothing specific to any Medicare contractor.
Nurse practitioners and physician assistants: enrollment requirements, supervision or collaboration documents, direct versus incident-to billing, plans that do not credential them.
Hospital, skilled nursing and other facility privileging and reappointment, which gates all facility-based work.

The rest of Medicare enrollment: group enrollment (CMS-855B), electronic funds transfer (CMS-588), participation agreement (CMS-460), PTANs, ordering and referring status, and the duty to report changes within 30 or 90 days.
Contracting and payment set-up after approval: contract execution, fee schedule loading, effective-date letters, EFT, ERA and EDI enrollment, directory listing.
Timely filing rules for held claims; what may be billed to patients (including Medicare and QMB patients) during a gap.
The actual denial reason and remark codes to monitor, by payer.
Provider departure and offboarding: ending reassignments, updating CAQH, notifying plans, tail coverage.
Ownership change, tax ID change or practice sale: enrollment and contract consequences (named only as an audit trigger).
Licence, DEA and controlled-substance renewal calendars, continuing education and training attestations, malpractice minimums.
Exclusion screening for staff, contractors and vendors; state exclusion lists.
State prompt-credentialing and provisional-credentialing laws; escalation routes such as a plan's provider advocate or the state insurance regulator.
Working files: no spreadsheet, payer contact list, follow-up script, retroactive-coverage letter or patient letter.
Cost, staffing time, and outsourcing versus in-house or software options; no source for any figure.
